The litigation problem

Clients pay to read the record. Almost none of it reaches the hearing.

Load the matter and Cicero reads every document in it. It maps the evidence to the issues, drafts the chronology and shows you where the witnesses disagree. Your team starts on the case, not the pile.

Result

The challenge

The other side produced 40,000 documents with the hearing three weeks out. Four lawyers, no time for a linear review and no budget for a review team.

The approach

The team loaded the production into Cicero and worked from the matter model. Every proposition was pulled out and attached to the issues in dispute and the people who made it, with contradictions flagged.

What they found

Eighteen documented reasons their client should not give evidence, each traced to its source. That changed the strategy for the hearing.

The outcome

A multimillion dollar difference in the result, found by four people in three weeks in a production designed to bury them.

The evolution of fact finding

Each generation of review technology narrowed what a human had to read. None of them built the case.

Under the hood

Every fact, filed where it belongs.

A witness statement isn't one thing. It's dozens of claims about who did what, and when. Cicero pulls out each one, works out which event it describes and which issue it goes to, and checks it against everything else the record says about that event.

StepLayerWhat Cicero does
01IssuesTurns the allegations and denials into a list of what is actually in dispute, and who is involved.
02PropositionsBreaks each document into its claims: who said what, when, where and to whom.
03EventsGroups claims about the same event, wherever they came from. When two accounts disagree, you see both.
04Work productDrafts the chronology, the issues and evidence matrices and the cast list, with a source on every line.
Ask the matter.

The Agent works from that structure, not a keyword index, so its answers draw on the whole record and every citation opens at the paragraph it relies on.

The Brief

Every issue, and where the evidence lands.

One page per dispute that tells you where you stand. The Agent reads it before it answers anything.

01Issue matrixEach issue, where the record lands on it, and the sub-issues argued for each side.
02Pleadings matrixEvery allegation and each party's response: admitted, denied or qualified.
03ChronologyEvents from across the record, with conflicting accounts marked.
04Key playersEveryone in the matter, ranked by how often the record mentions them.

Chronology

Every date in dispute, and who disputes it.

Cicero groups every proposition into events and puts them in date order. Where accounts of an event differ, both sit on the entry with their sources. Export it as the schedule for the hearing.

01One entry per eventEverything the record says about an event sits on one entry, whichever documents it came from.
02Conflicts shownWhere two accounts differ, both appear, with the paragraph each one comes from.
03Cut by issueFilter to the events that matter for one issue, one person or one month.
04Any languageEntries draw on documents in every language in the record, each tied to its original.

The Agent

Ask the hard questions. Check every answer.

Built for evidence, not legal research. The Agent uses the matter model to decide which documents to read, so it works across the whole record rather than whatever a search happened to return.

04Hands you a draftAsk for a Word document and you get one.

Where Cicero fits in EDRM 2.0

Analysis is no longer a step. It runs beneath every stage.

EDRM 2.0 (2025) restructures the industry-standard e-Discovery Reference Model. Analysis is no longer one step between processing and review. It is a continuous layer beneath every stage.

Cicero is built for that layer. It turns the record into the matter map and the work product while review is still under way, not after it.

What you're looking at

Two languages, one event, and a date nobody agrees on.

A chronology entry in Cicero. The Employer's witness statement, in English, puts the site handover on February 19, 2024. Translated from Arabic, the Engineer's letter and the signed handover record both say March 3. Cicero puts all three accounts on the same event and flags the conflict.

How it works

Built for records that cross languages.

Both directions

Translate documents into the language your team works in, and work product into the language the tribunal wants.

Analyzed in the original

Documents are analyzed in the language they were written in, so propositions, events and key players come from the source text, not from a translation of it.

Linked to the source

Every translated passage stays linked to its original paragraph. When it matters what a document actually says, the source is one click away.

One chronology

Events draw on documents in every language in the record. When accounts in different languages disagree, the contradiction is flagged like any other.

Languages

The languages your matters run in.

Spotlight: Arabic

Arabic and English. One record.

← Insights
Essay

Matter analysis, a category of its own.

eDiscovery holds the record. General-purpose AI drafts and researches. Neither builds the case.

By
Joe Rayment, Founder and CEO
Reading time
4 minutes

Every disputes team now runs two kinds of software. An eDiscovery platform holds, processes and produces the record. A firm-wide AI platform drafts, summarizes and researches. Both are useful. Neither does the work that decides most disputes.

That work sits between them. Someone has to read the record against the pleadings, work out what each document says about each issue, notice when two witnesses describe the same meeting differently, and turn all of it into a chronology and an evidence matrix the team can rely on. Today that someone is usually a junior lawyer with a spreadsheet and a deadline.

We call that work matter analysis. It deserves a category of its own for three reasons.

What is the unit of work?

In eDiscovery the unit is the document. Is it responsive, is it privileged, does it go out. In general-purpose AI the unit is the prompt. In matter analysis the unit is the proposition: who said what, when, to whom, and which issue it bears on. Change the unit and you change what the software can do. Propositions can be grouped into events, compared with each other and tested against the pleadings.

What does it produce?

Review produces a set of documents. A chat produces an answer. Matter analysis produces the work product litigators already use: the pleadings matrix, the chronology, the issues and evidence matrices, the dramatis personae. Each line links to its source, so it can be checked and defended.

Review answers which documents a person should read. Matter analysis answers what the documents mean for the case.

Where does it sit?

The industry's own reference model has caught up. EDRM 2.0 treats analysis as a continuous layer beneath every stage, rather than one step between processing and review. Matter analysis is that layer. It reads the collection your eDiscovery platform supplies, and its source-linked outputs can be interrogated by the AI tools your firm already owns. See where Cicero sits in EDRM 2.0.

The point of naming it is practical. Firms buying AI for disputes have been asked to choose between review platforms that do not build the case and generalist tools that cannot make it defensible. They do not have to choose. Matter analysis is the missing layer, and it decides who understands the case first.

← Insights
Essay

The case is the output.

Every generation of review technology narrowed what a lawyer had to read. None of them built the case.

By
Joe Rayment, Founder and CEO
Reading time
4 minutes

Litigation has a strange economy. We pay lawyers to read the record, and then almost none of the record matters.

RAND found that 73% of e-discovery spend goes on review.1 Collection and processing are small change by comparison. A survey of major US companies put the ratio of pages produced to pages used at trial at 1,044 to one.2 The Australian Law Reform Commission reported a case where 200,000 documents were discovered and 50 were admitted. None of the 50 was determinative.3

So the expensive part is the reading. And most of the reading is wasted.

Each wave of technology went after the waste. Search terms cut the pile, and missed anything not on the list. Predictive coding ranked documents by similarity to earlier decisions. Efficient, and blind to meaning. Generative AI let you ask a question and get an answer citing a handful of documents. Fast, and unstructured.

All of them answer the same question. Which documents should a person read? That is a useful question. It is not the case.

The case is a set of issues, the facts that bear on them, and the places where accounts of the same event disagree.

Today a team builds that by hand after review closes, against the hearing timetable. That is where the weekends go.

Cicero builds it from the record. The allegations and denials define the issues. Every document is broken into propositions: who said what, when, where and to whom. Those propositions are grouped into events and attached to the issues and the people. Where two accounts of the same event differ, Cicero flags it.

The chronology, the issues matrix, the evidence matrix and the key players come out the other end. Every line links to its source.

That changes what a lawyer does with their time. Less finding. More judgment.

It also changes who can win. If understanding the record no longer depends on how many people you can put on it, the case turns more on its merits. That is the point of the whole thing.

  1. RAND Institute for Civil Justice, Where the Money Goes (2012)
  2. Lawyers for Civil Justice, Civil Justice Reform Group and US Chamber Institute for Legal Reform, Litigation Cost Survey of Major Companies (2010)
  3. Australian Law Reform Commission, Managing Discovery, Report 115 (2011), paras 3.49 and 3.53
← Insights
Essay

Mostly right is not good enough.

Generalist AI is becoming the base layer of every firm. Litigation still needs a specialist on top.

By
Joe Rayment, Founder and CEO
Reading time
3 minutes

Every large firm now has a generalist AI platform. It drafts, summarizes, researches and answers email. That is a good thing, and it is not going away.

The question is what sits on top of it for litigation.

In most practice areas a fluent first draft is the job. A lawyer reads it, fixes it and sends it. In litigation the output has to survive the other side, and then a judge. Mostly right is not a standard you can run a hearing on.

Generalist tools organize around the prompt. The user supplies the structure every time. The output is prose, and prose has to be checked line by line before anyone relies on it. Ask the same question twice and you can get two different answers. In a contract review that is an inconvenience. In evidence it is a risk.

Litigation already has a structure. The tools should start from it.

Issues come from the pleadings. Facts attach to issues. Witnesses contradict each other, and sometimes themselves. The work product has conventions everyone in the room understands: the chronology, the issues matrix, the evidence matrix, the list of key players.

A specialist platform builds that structure from the record once and keeps it. Every answer draws on the whole matter. Every citation can be checked against the document. The lawyer starts from a built case rather than a blank prompt.

This is the pattern I expect to hold. A generalist base layer for every lawyer in the firm. Specialist platforms for the work the generalist cannot make defensible. Litigation is the clearest example.

The firms getting this right are not choosing one or the other. They run both, and they are clear about which job each one does.

Essay

One record, many languages.

Disputes in the Gulf rarely run in one language. Most tools still do.

By
Joe Rayment, Founder and CEO
Reading time
3 minutes

A construction dispute in Riyadh or Dubai rarely runs in one language. The contract is in Arabic. The site correspondence is in English. The witness statements come in both, and the tribunal may want the bundle in either.

Most teams handle this with a translation vendor and a lot of patience. Documents go out, translations come back, and the analysis starts once everything is in one language. By then the timetable has moved on.

Translation alone doesn't solve the problem. A translated document is still just a document. Someone has to read it, work out what it says about the issues, and notice when it contradicts something written in the other language.

The contradiction that matters is often the one that crosses languages.

Cicero now translates the record across languages, starting with the pair Gulf disputes need most. Documents translate from Arabic to English and from English to Arabic. Arabic documents are analyzed in the original, so propositions come from the Arabic text rather than from a translation of it. When the Engineer's letter in Arabic and the Employer's witness statement in English give different dates for the same event, the conflict shows up on one line of the chronology.

Every translated passage stays tied to the original. When it matters what the Arabic actually says, the source is one click away.

The same works for French, German, Spanish, Portuguese and the other languages a record tends to arrive in.

Where the platform runs matters as much as what it does. Cicero is hosted in the UAE and seven other regions, so client data stays in the jurisdiction it belongs in.

Cross-border disputes are where the gap between well-resourced and stretched teams is widest. Language shouldn't be the reason a team runs out of time before it runs out of case.

← Insights
Guide

Twelve questions to ask before you buy litigation AI.

A short list for disputes partners and innovation teams. The answers separate tools you can rely on in a hearing from tools you will end up re-checking.

By
Joe Rayment, Founder and CEO
Reading time
5 minutes

Most demonstrations of legal AI look good. The differences show up later, on a live matter, when someone has to rely on the output. These questions are designed to surface those differences early.

  1. Can every answer be checked against the document?If a citation cannot be opened at the paragraph it relies on, someone will have to re-read the source anyway.
  2. What did it read but not cite?A tool that shows only what it cited hides what it weighed and discarded. That is where missed evidence lives.
  3. Does it work across the whole record, or a sample of it?Retrieval that pulls a handful of passages into a context window misses whatever it never retrieved. Ask how it decides what to read.
  4. Is the output work product or prose?A pleadings matrix, a chronology and an evidence matrix can be checked line by line. Paragraphs of fluent prose cannot.
  5. Will it give the same answer twice?Run the same question on the same documents a week apart. Variation that is tolerable in drafting is a risk in evidence.
  6. Does it start from the issues in dispute?Analysis organized around the allegations and denials stays relevant. Analysis organized around keywords drifts.
  7. How does it handle other languages?If part of the record is in Arabic or another language, ask whether it is analyzed in the original and whether translations stay linked to the source.
  8. Where is the data hosted?Ask which jurisdiction the data sits in, who operates the infrastructure, and whether you can choose.
  9. Which certifications are independently audited?ISO 27001, ISO 42001 and SOC 2 Type II reports are evidence. A security page is not.
  10. How does the price behave as the matter grows?Per-query and per-token pricing can make the largest matters the most expensive to analyze properly. Ask for the price of a matter twice the size.
  11. Can you run it on a live matter first?A demonstration on a curated data set tells you little. A working session on your own documents tells you a lot.
  12. What leaves with you?Exports to Word, Excel and your review platform should be complete, so the work product stays yours.
← Insights Methodology note

Four ways to run a review, and what the studies show.

Prepared by
Automatise
Date
October 2026
Contents
01 Summary
02 Four ways to run a review
03 Three kinds of machine
04 What published studies report
01

Summary.

Review technology answers one question: which documents should a person read? This note compares the four standard ways of answering it, and what the published studies say about how well generative AI does.

Cicero works on the next question, which is what those documents mean for the case. That is why the comparison matters to us: the better the review, the better the record Cicero starts from.

02

Four ways to run a review.

The standard industry comparison.

DimensionPrioritized linearTAR 1.0TAR 2.0Generative AI
GoalHumans review every document, in the most efficient orderSplit the corpus into responsive and not, with the fewest human decisionsHuman review of responsive documents only, without touching the full corpusTune the tag descriptions, then let the AI review the whole population
Review strategyHighest-scoring first, until everything is reviewedBorderline documents first, to push them to one side or the otherHighest-scoring first, until the required recall is reachedSmall random samples to tune prompts until precision and recall targets are met
After reviewReady for productionModel-responsive documents usually get a full human reviewReady for productionAI-responsive documents ready for production, minus privilege hits
Target metricsPrecision and recall not measuredPrecision 40%+, recall 75%Precision not measured, recall 75%Precision 75%, recall 75%

As presented at an eDiscovery vendor briefing, 2026.

03

Three kinds of machine.

TAR ranks. Generative AI reads. Cicero builds. The analogies the market uses, and the one that fits Cicero.

TAR

Machine learning that learns from prior coding decisions and ranks the rest of the corpus by similarity.

Like a streaming service's recommendations: it learns what you liked and finds more of it. Good at more of the same. Silent on why.
GenAI review

A language model applies a written description to unreviewed documents and decides whether each tag applies.

Like a well-read editor skimming thousands of articles for the ones that match your brief. Fast, articulate, and the output is still a pile of documents.
Cicero

Pulls the evidentiary propositions out of every document and attaches them to the issues, events and people in the matter.

Like a junior who has read everything, then hands you the chronology, the issues matrix and the witness list with a page reference on every line.
04

What published studies report.

Recall is the share of the relevant documents a review finds. Precision is the share of the documents it marks relevant that really are. These are the published figures for generative AI review, with the classic TAR benchmark alongside.

StudyReviewDataRecallPrecision
Grossman and Cormack, 20111TAR, TREC 2009 Legal TrackEnron, 836,165 documents, five topics76.7%84.7%
Grossman and Cormack, 20111Exhaustive manual reviewSame topics59.3%31.7%
Omrani et al., 2024 (Relativity)2GPT-4133,638 documents, live civil matter96%60%
Everlaw, 20243Generative AI coding suggestions7,737 documents, four civil matters89%67%
Keeling et al., 20264Relativity aiR for Review1,600 documents, regulatory subpoena83.9%84.7%
Redgrave LLP, 2026, working paper5Relativity aiR for Review45,004 public documents, blinded expert88%29%
Redgrave LLP, 2026, working paper5Active learning (TAR 2.0)Same documents64%39%

Across the four generative AI studies, recall averages 89% and precision 60%. Against the targets typically set for TAR, 75% recall and, for TAR 1.0, 40% precision, that is 19% better recall and 50% better precision. Courts have treated recall of 70% to 80% as consistent with an adequate review.6

Precision varies far more than recall, because it depends on how many documents in a set are relevant and how borderline calls are counted. The one head-to-head study found generative AI less precise than active learning, 29% against 39%, while finding far more of the relevant documents.

Most published generative AI figures come from vendors or test one vendor's tool, and every study measures against human coding that is itself imperfect. Figures from different matters are not directly comparable.

  1. Maura R. Grossman and Gordon V. Cormack, Technology-Assisted Review in E-Discovery Can Be More Effective and More Efficient Than Exhaustive Manual Review, 17 Richmond Journal of Law and Technology 11 (2011)
  2. Omrani et al., Beyond the Bar: Generative AI as a Transformative Component in Legal Document Review, Relativity (2024)
  3. Everlaw, GenAI document review surpasses human performance on real-world litigation (September 19, 2024)
  4. Robert Keeling, Ray Mangum, Amy Hanke and Alyssa Ogden, Journal of Technology Law and Policy, vol. 30 (2026)
  5. Redgrave LLP, What a major study shows about gen AI and TAR in a complex document review (June 2026)
  6. In re Broiler Chicken Antitrust Litigation, N.D. Ill., order of January 3, 2018
